::: {.why}
Splitting the decision into a primary model that picks direction and a secondary model that decides size is a structure that fits how a desk actually works, and it lets a weak signal keep its direction while a model sizes it.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Implement meta-labelling on top of an existing signal and report the change in precision and in information ratio.
- Say why the secondary model is a better-posed problem than predicting direction directly.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [35 min]{.task-min} Build it: take one existing signal as the primary model, label each of its calls as correct or not using the triple-barrier outcome, and fit a classifier to predict that. Size the position by the classifier's predicted probability. Report precision, recall and information ratio against the unmetalabelled version.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Say why it can work: the secondary problem is binary, balanced by construction, and conditions on a decision already made, so the model is estimating a conditional probability rather than a direction in a near-zero-signal cross-section. Then note the failure mode, which is that the secondary model can learn to switch the primary off entirely in the regimes where its training data was thinnest.
:::
:::
